query: Which method can be used for high-temperature oxidation behaviour and phase stability, and why?

generation.hypothesis: When a Ni–Cr alloy is heated in an oxidizing atmosphere, in-situ thermogravimetric analysis (TGA) can measure a progressive mass gain corresponding to oxide formation, and subsequent X-ray diffraction (XRD) will confirm the presence and stability of chromia-based protective layers at high temperature.
generation.material_initial_state: A Ni–Cr alloy sample (e.g., ~20% Cr), polished and free of surface scale before testing.
generation.intervention: Subject the Ni–Cr alloy to a controlled heating program (e.g., 10 °C/min) in an oxidizing environment while monitoring mass changes by TGA, followed by XRD characterization.
generation.conditions: Heated in air from room temperature up to 1100 °C, with holding steps at selected temperatures for phase analysis.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a chromia-based oxide layer on the alloy surface during exposure to high temperature in an oxidizing atmosphere.
generation.mechanism: The protective chromia-based scale forms on the surface, limiting oxygen diffusion into the alloy and thus slowing further oxidation.
generation.predicted_outcome: A measurable increase in mass due to oxidation (detected via TGA) that saturates once a protective oxide layer has formed, verified by identifying stable oxide phases (chromia or spinel structures) via XRD.
generation.baseline: Without an oxygen-containing atmosphere, the alloy displays negligible mass gain and no new oxide phases form.
generation.boundary: Alloys with insufficient Cr content (<10%) may not form a continuous protective oxide scale and may undergo more severe oxidation; TGA and XRD results may vary with oxidizing conditions and alloy composition.
generation.uncertainty: Exact growth kinetics and final oxide phase composition may differ under varying oxygen partial pressures, heating rates, and specific alloy chemistries.

falsification_experiment.design: Conduct multiple TGA/XRD cycles at different oxygen partial pressures (e.g., 1%, 10%, and 21% O2) and measure both mass changes and oxide phases formed.
measurements: In-situ or post-experiment X-ray diffraction patterns to identify oxide phases
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the mass gain does not correlate with the oxygen partial pressure or if no stable oxide phases (e.g., chromia) are detected via XRD, the hypothesis that TGA and XRD can reliably determine high-temperature oxidation behavior and phase stability in Ni–Cr alloys would be refuted.
